items.abstract: <jats:p>Operations management in media plays a critical role in reshaping how content is produced, structured, and optimized for generative search engines and agentic AI systems. In this context, operations management is no longer limited to coordinating workflows or supervising editorial processes; it has become a strategic intelligence layer that connects content architecture, data engineering, and algorithmic behavior. Modern media operations focus on designing intelligent workflows that ensure content is machine-readable, semantically structured, and contextually optimized. This includes the use of metadata frameworks, hierarchical information design, and semantic tagging systems that allow generative search engines to interpret, summarize, and recompose content into direct, AI-generated answers. As a result, content visibility is no longer determined only by traditional SEO factors, but by how well it aligns with generative interpretation models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. At the same time, operations management enables the integration of agentic AI systems into media ecosystems, transforming them into semi-autonomous operational environments. These agentic systems can analyze performance data, monitor audience behavior, and adjust content distribution strategies in real time without continuous human intervention. In this structure, operations management acts as a supervisory intelligence layer that defines goals,</jats:p>
title: Operations Management in Digital Media and Public Relations: AI Agents and the Evolution of Search Visibility

items.abstract:
<jats:p><p>The opacity of an autonomous AI agent is routinely discussed as a single "black box" problem, to be reduced by interpretability research or by demands for transparency. This paper argues that the opacity has two architecturally distinct causes that the discourse conflates, and that the conflation is what makes the transparency debate unwinnable. One cause is technical: behavior internalized into model weights cannot be read, versioned, or reverted without retraining. The other is commercial: the human-built layer around the weights — system prompts, rules, tool definitions, the agent loop — is technically inspectable but kept proprietary because it is a competitive differentiator. The two causes admit different responses, and treating them as one problem routes every transparency argument into an irresolvable safety-versus-secrecy collision.</p>
<p>The paper makes three contributions, drawn from the implementation history of a single agent and re-expressed as harness-neutral judgments. First, it grounds the opacity problem in an accountability gap: a text-based prohibition on a capability that physically exists is a signpost, not a control, and enforcement admits a prohibition-strength hierarchy — absence, then scaffolding-layer enforcement, then untrusted-content boundary — most published safety work occupying only the weakest layer. Second, it separates the two-layer black box: technical internalization (Layer 1, largely permanent) from commercial secrecy of scaffolding (Layer 2, contingent on market structure). Third, it resolves Layer 2 with a minimum disclosure set: operator visibility is decoupled from public disclosure, and the minimum that makes post-incident causal tracing possible — which scaffolding version was active, which inputs reached the agent, which approval gated the version — is disclosable without publishing the scaffolding text.</p>
<p>The resolution is implementable with current technology; it waits on neither an interpretability breakthrough nor a restructuring of markets and law. It complements existing AI risk-management and management-system standards by naming the operator-visibility floor those standards presuppose. The open questions — where exactly the disclosure line falls, and how the technology–society timescale gap is to be managed — are the research agenda.</p></jats:p>
title: The Two-Layer Black Box: Operator Visibility, Commercial Secrecy, and a Minimum Disclosure Set for Accountable Autonomous AI Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper introduces <b>political visibility</b> as a foundational concept for democratic theory in the AI age, and argues that the progressive migration of political decisions into AI infrastructure constitutes a historically distinctive mechanism of democratic hollowing-out. Political visibility is defined as the condition in which the decisions that constitute collective governance occur within a public domain that is identifiable, contestable, participable, and accountable. These four dimensions are not procedural niceties but necessary conditions of democratic legitimacy: the absence of any single dimension is sufficient to produce a visibility deficit that no institutional form of democracy can compensate. The paper distinguishes political visibility from the established tradition of the "politics of visibility"-which concerns who is seen within politics and argues that the present crisis concerns whether politics itself remains visible at all. The central argument is that AI infrastructure systems-foundation models, recommendation architectures, RLHF alignment procedures, and government AI procurement-constitute a new mechanism of the infrastructuralisation of politics: the migration of substantive political decisions from visible democratic governance into a technical layer that is structurally beyond the reach of democratic procedure. Drawing on the infrastructure studies tradition (Bowker and Star; Larkin; Plantin et al.), the paper identifies how this mechanism operates, situates it within the established hollowing-out thesis (Mair; Crouch; Wolin; Brown; Urbinati), and identifies what is historically distinctive about its AI-age instantiation. The paper closes by positioning political visibility as the first principle from which AI-era democratic governance must be reconstructed, and previews a broader research programme in AI-era state theory.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>AI-mediated discovery systems have fundamentally altered the conditions under which organizational brand visibility is produced and maintained. Where traditional search environments rewarded ranking optimization, AI systems reconstruct brand representations from distributed signals-synthesizing content, structured data, thirdparty sources, and historical signals into responses that users receive without visiting organizational properties. This shift produces a zero-click visibility problem: organizations influence decisions they cannot observe, through representations they do not control, in systems they cannot audit directly. This paper introduces the Brand Visibility Maturity Model (BVMM), a governance framework that assesses how effectively organizations govern the signals that AI systems use to construct their brand representations. Drawing on capability maturity modeling in the CMMI tradition, the BVMM evaluates governance maturity across seven domains-Content, SEO, AI Governance, Accessibility, Website Performance, Local Visibility, and International Visibility-using a five-level behavioral maturity scale. The framework is positioned at the intersection of platform governance, information retrieval, algorithmic accountability, and organizational governance theory. Its primary application is as a teaching instrument in postgraduate programs addressing AI-mediated visibility governance, and as a professional assessment tool for organizations seeking to evaluate and improve their governance posture in an AI-mediated discovery environment.</jats:p>
title: The Brand Visibility Maturity Model: A Governance Framework for AI-Mediated Organizational Visibility

<jats:p><p>The rise of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok has redefined digital discovery, shifting user behavior away from search engines toward AI assistants as the first layer of recommendation and decision-making. Traditional SEO frameworks, built on backlinks, keywords, and domain authority, no longer guarantee visibility in AI-mediated environments. To address this gap, the AIVO Standard™ (AI Visibility Optimization) introduces a structured, certifiable methodology to ensure products, services, and organizations are discoverable, recommendable, and trusted within AI ecosystems.</p>
<p>Version 3.0 of the AIVO Standard marks a pivotal evolution of the framework. Beyond its nine-stage methodology—spanning foundational presence, knowledge graph expansion, prompt discoverability, multi-modal content readiness, and trust signal integration—it introduces a quantification layer through the<span>&nbsp;</span><strong>Prompt-Space Occupancy Score (PSOS™)</strong>. PSOS functions as the first governance-ready KPI for AI visibility, translating prompt-level performance into a board-ready score with two complementary modes: (i) Enterprise Mode, based on direct prompt-cluster testing across multiple AI engines with confidence intervals and provenance logging; and (ii) Local/SME Mode, based on evidence proxies such as citations, reviews, freshness, and offline credibility.</p>
<p>This edition emphasizes governance, reproducibility, and financial attribution, linking PSOS shifts to measurable business outcomes through causal attribution modeling. By establishing both operational best practices and quantifiable benchmarks, AIVO Standard™ v3.0 advances AI discoverability from an ad hoc set of tactics into a measurable, auditable discipline—positioned for compliance integration, venture due diligence, and global digital trust standards.</p></jats:p>
title: Methodology for AI Visibility Optimization Version 3.0

items.abstract:
<jats:p><p>AI-generated answers change how visibility is determined because the system interprets a query, selects sources, and generates a response before the user clicks. This shifts visibility away from ranking position alone and toward observable system behaviour inside generated answers.</p>
<p>This paper defines a framework for evaluating AI visibility through four outcome layers: AI referral traffic, AI search inclusion, AI brand mentions, and AI recommendation behaviour. It separates these outcome signals from diagnostic signals such as source page count, entity clarity, authority and trust, and technical readiness.</p>
<p>The framework is applied to a controlled university prompt dataset across multiple AI systems to demonstrate how visibility behaves in practice. The results show that visibility concentrates around a limited set of sources and that inclusion, attribution, and recommendation operate as distinct behaviours that require separate measurement.</p></jats:p>
title: A Framework for Evaluating AI Search Visibility Signals

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Population-level data for animals in commercial industries are rarely accessible to independent researchers. While animal-reliant industries may nominally disclose information via public registries, practical barriers such as dated interfaces, scattered sources, and reluctance to share data directly often prevent meaningful independent welfare oversight. This paper describes a novel methodology using agentic artificial intelligence (specifically, AI agents) to assemble a population-level dataset from publicly accessible registries, with greyhound racing under licensed regulation in the UK as a case study. A dataset of 31,028 individual greyhounds was assembled through cross-referencing of the Irish Coursing Club Stud Book, dog profiles, and race histories from the Greyhound Board of Great Britain (GBGB) racing database,
                    <jats:ext-link>www.Greyhound-Data.com</jats:ext-link>
                    ,
                    <jats:ext-link>www.Greyhoundstats.co.uk</jats:ext-link>
                    , and the British Greyhound Stud Book, achieving 99.3% resolution of greyhound origin classifications. This provides census-level representation of the licensed greyhound racing population and data from 1,267,119 individual race entries between January 2022 and March 2026. AI agent-assisted collation under human oversight enabled data assembly at a scale and timeframe that would otherwise have been prohibitive. Dog identifiers were replaced with numerical codes in the deposited dataset, and human identifiers were removed. The dataset revealed that 85.1% of dogs racing in the UK in 2025 were Irish-bred, the median duration of active racing before exiting the industry was 30 starts across 11.9 months, and the rate at which dogs exit racing has not changed since 2022. Most inactive dogs have no traceable, publicly documented post-racing outcome. The GBGB holds unpublished data on retirement destinations, career-ending reasons, and individual-level injury and euthanasia figures—a structured visibility absence and an animal welfare concern. Where industries curate their own transparency, this AI agent-assisted collation method shows that independently assembled evidence can reveal what selective disclosure obscures. In doing so, it removes a practical barrier to the evidence-based accountability that social license and animal welfare improvement require. This approach, which includes ethical considerations and accountability, is replicable across other animal-reliant industries. Where population-level welfare data are not easily visible, this method has the potential to substantially expand the evidence base available to welfare scientists, regulators, policymakers, and the public.
                  </jats:p>
title: Using AI agents to assemble population-level data for visibility and animal welfare insights: a case study of greyhound racing in the UK

<jats:p><p>AI-generated answers are changing how prospective students discover and evaluate universities because systems interpret queries, select sources, and construct responses before a user visits a website. This shifts visibility from ranking position alone to observable behaviour within generated outputs, where inclusion, attribution, and recommendation determine which institutions are considered.</p>
<p>This paper presents an applied framework for evaluating university AI search visibility using four outcome layers: AI search inclusion, AI brand mentions, AI recommendation behaviour, and AI referral traffic. The study applies this framework to a controlled dataset of Computer Science queries executed across multiple AI systems, including ChatGPT, Google AI Overview, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini, and Grok.</p>
<p>The results show that visibility is concentrated among a limited set of universities, with repeated inclusion and recommendation driven by content structure, entity clarity, and external reinforcement rather than traditional ranking position alone. Institutions that provide structured, topic-aligned content and maintain consistent representation across external sources are more likely to be selected and recommended within generated answers.</p>
<p>The findings demonstrate that university visibility is increasingly determined at the point of answer construction. This requires a shift from ranking-focused optimisation to content and entity strategies aligned with how AI systems interpret, synthesise, and present information during student discovery.</p></jats:p>
title: A Framework for Evaluating University AI Search Visibility Signals
